lines.say: Play a chord on a piano. How does your ear pick out the notes?
One tangled wave reaches you, yet you hear three separate notes.
Your ear splits the wave into the frequencies inside it. That's a Fourier transform.
The quantum Fourier transform, or Q F T, does the same to amplitudes, the numbers that set each reading's chance.
Two qubits have four possible readings: zero, one, two and three.
Put equal weight on zero and two, and none on one or three. It repeats every two steps.
Run the Q F T, and the output peaks at zero and two, matching that rhythm.
Here's why. Each input sends an arrow to every output, and the way it points is called its phase.
From zero, the arrows all point up. From two, they flip half a turn at every step.
At one and three, the arrows point opposite ways and cancel. At zero and two, they add. That's interference.
Slide the pattern onto one and three, and the peaks stay put. The Q F T hears the rhythm.
Here the chord picture breaks. Your ear hears every note at once.
Measure afterwards, and you get one frequency per run, picked at random from the peaks.
So it isn't a faster way to analyse data. It shines when you need one hidden rhythm.
That's the step at the heart of Shor's algorithm for factoring big numbers.
So the Q F T turns rhythm into position. With N readings, a pattern repeating every r steps lands on multiples of N over r.
